title: Habits and motivation
keyIdea: A habit is a loop: a cue triggers a routine, and a reward makes your brain want to repeat it. You build good habits by making them easy to start and linking them to a clear cue. Making bad habits awkward helps more than relying on willpower. Habits take weeks to feel automatic, often about two months, and one missed day barely matters. Inside (intrinsic) motivation, doing something because you value it, lasts longer than outside rewards and punishments. Putting things off is mostly a way to escape a bad feeling, so starting small helps. People keep going when they feel choice, skill and connection.

kid: A habit is something you do almost without thinking. Every habit runs on a loop. First comes a cue, a trigger such as your phone buzzing or getting home from school. Then the routine, the thing you do, such as checking the app or grabbing a snack. Last comes the reward, the good feeling, which teaches your brain to repeat the routine next time the cue appears.

Willpower is weakest when you are tired, hungry or stressed. So change your surroundings instead. Put the guitar on a stand where you can see it, and charge your phone in another room. If a good habit takes one easy step to start and a bad habit takes several awkward steps, the good one wins on tired nights. New habits take time. You may have heard 21 days, but that is a myth. In a 2010 study, the middle person took 66 days for a daily habit to feel automatic, and some took 254. Missing one day hardly made a difference, so if you slip, just carry on tomorrow.

Motivation can come from inside or outside. Inside (intrinsic) motivation means you do it because you enjoy it or care about it. Outside (extrinsic) motivation means you do it for a prize, money or to avoid trouble. Prizes can help with dull jobs, but paying someone for something they already love can make them enjoy it less. People also keep going when they feel three things: choice (autonomy), getting better at it (competence) and being with others (relatedness).

Putting things off is not laziness. Usually a task makes you feel bored, worried or unsure, and delaying it gives quick relief. The bad feeling comes back bigger as the deadline gets closer. Starting for just two minutes often shrinks the feeling.
adult: This topic is for ages 12 to 13. It covers how habits form and what keeps people motivated. A habit is a loop of cue, routine and reward. It becomes automatic when it is repeated in the same setting. In a 2010 study, Lally and colleagues asked people to take up one daily habit. The middle time to reach 95% of their top automatic level was 66 days. The range was 18 to 254 days. Missing one day did not set people back. The popular 21-day rule has no good evidence.

Good habit design uses cues and friction. Tie the new habit to a cue that already happens, make it easy to start, and put barriers in front of the habits you want to drop. This works better than willpower, which is weakest when people are tired or stressed. In the lab, each evening compares Ravi's energy with the effort it takes to start.

Intrinsic motivation means doing something because you value it. Extrinsic motivation means doing it for a reward or to avoid a punishment. Rewards can help people start dull tasks. But an expected prize for something a child already enjoys can make them choose it less later. This is the overjustification effect. Lepper, Greene and Nisbett showed it in 1973 with young children who were promised a certificate for drawing. Self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000) says motivation lasts when three needs are met: autonomy, competence and relatedness.

Common mistakes: seeing procrastination as poor time management, when it is mostly a quick fix for a bad mood (Sirois and Pychyl, 2013); believing habits form in exactly 21 days; giving up after one missed day; and thinking more rewards always mean more motivation. Help young people notice the feeling that makes them delay. Then agree a two-minute start on the task.

familyTip: Pick one small habit to build together, like a ten-minute tidy after dinner. Agree on the cue that starts it, make it easy to begin, and track it on a calendar for two months. If someone misses a day, just carry on the next day.

practice.prompt: Each time Leah sits on the bus, she puts her earphones in and plays a game. What is the cue in this habit?
choices: Sitting on the bus
Playing the game
Enjoying the game
practice.hint: The cue is the trigger that comes first.
practice.explain: Sitting on the bus is the cue. Playing is the routine and the fun is the reward.

practice.prompt: Omar wants to read for {n} minutes each night but keeps scrolling instead. Which change helps most?
choices: Put the book on his pillow and charge the phone in another room
Promise himself he will try harder
Wait until he feels like reading
practice.hint: Make the good habit easy and the bad one awkward.
practice.explain: With the book on his pillow and the phone out of reach, {n} minutes of reading is the easiest choice on a tired night. Willpower alone often fails.

practice.prompt: Priya has done her new morning stretch for {d} days. It still does not feel automatic. What is most likely?
choices: That is normal: habits often take about two months or more
She is doing it wrong
Habits always form in 21 days, so she has failed
practice.hint: How long did the middle person take in the 2010 study?
practice.explain: After {d} days a habit often still needs effort. In the study the middle time was 66 days, from 18 to 254, so she should keep going.

practice.prompt: Which is an inside (intrinsic) reason for playing the piano?
choices: She loves how the music sounds
Her parents pay her
She wants to avoid being told off
practice.hint: Is the reward the activity itself, or something outside it?
practice.explain: Loving the sound is an inside reason: the playing is its own reward. Money and avoiding trouble are outside reasons.

practice.prompt: Jay has an essay due in {d} days. Every time he opens it he feels worried, so he watches videos instead. What is really going on?
choices: He is escaping a bad feeling for quick relief
He has too little time
He does not care about school
practice.hint: Think about what changes in how he feels when he delays.
practice.explain: Watching videos gives quick relief from the worry. With {d} days left, the feeling will come back bigger. Starting for two minutes can shrink it.

pool.prompt: What is the correct order of a habit loop?
choices: Cue, routine, reward
Reward, cue, routine
Routine, reward, cue
pool.hint: What comes first and starts the habit?
pool.explain: A cue triggers the routine, and the reward makes your brain want to repeat it.

pool.prompt: Ella wants to drink more water. Which plan is best?
choices: Fill a bottle each night and leave it by her school bag
Try to remember when she is thirsty
Wait until she is in the mood
pool.hint: Link it to a clear cue and make it easy to start.
pool.explain: Leaving a full bottle by her bag gives a clear cue and makes drinking water the easy choice.

pool.prompt: Sam missed his new habit on day {d}. What should he do?
choices: Carry on the next day: one miss barely matters
Start again from day 1
Give up, because the habit is ruined
pool.hint: What did the 2010 study find about missing one day?
pool.explain: Missing day {d} hardly changes how automatic the habit gets. Carrying on is what counts.

pool.prompt: Children who loved drawing were promised a prize for drawing. Later, with no prize, what happened?
choices: They chose to draw less than children who got no prize
They drew more than ever
Nothing changed
pool.hint: Can an outside reward crowd out an inside one?
pool.explain: The expected prize made drawing feel like work, so they drew less later. This is called the overjustification effect.

pool.prompt: Why do people often put off tasks they care about?
choices: To escape an uncomfortable feeling now
Because they are lazy
Because they cannot tell the time
pool.hint: Think of procrastination as a mood problem, not a time problem.
pool.explain: Delaying gives quick relief from feeling bored, worried or unsure. That is why it is a mood problem, not laziness.

pool.prompt: A club lets members choose projects, sets tasks they can just manage and works in teams. Which needs does it meet?
choices: Autonomy, competence and relatedness
Only competence
None, because there are no prizes
pool.hint: Choice, skill and connection: which of these are there?
pool.explain: Choosing projects is autonomy, tasks they can manage build competence, and teams give relatedness.

pool.prompt: Noah's parents offer £{n} for every hour he spends on his favourite hobby, drawing. What is a risk?
choices: He may start drawing for the money and enjoy it less
Nothing, because rewards always help
He will want to draw forever
pool.hint: What can an outside reward do to an inside reason?
pool.explain: Paying £{n} for something he already loves can turn it into a job, so he may enjoy it less when the money stops.

pool.prompt: Zoe has {d} days until a project is due and keeps avoiding it. Which first step helps most?
choices: Work on it for just two minutes now
Wait until she feels ready
Plan to do it all the night before
pool.hint: What shrinks the bad feeling that causes delay?
pool.explain: Starting for two minutes makes the task feel doable and shrinks the dread. Waiting lets the feeling grow over {d} days.

visual.caption: Inside or outside reason? Ask: is the activity its own reward?

items: Reading because the story is gripping
Practising because you love the sound
Running because it clears your head
Training only to win a medal

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build habit loops, redesign a room, drag the real habit curve, sort reasons, watch procrastination's mood swing and meet three needs.
